title: Roy Palmer as teacher; the New Orleans clique and Oliver's band split
summary: He hears Roy Palmer at his mother's fish fries, lists Palmer's pupils, and explains how the New Orleans musicians in Chicago fell out over Oliver's recordings.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: Well, what about before you went to school? Did you hear any music?

Yeah. Well, sometime my mother would have a fish fry and she was engaged with Roy Palmer. He had a friend that played a mountain. Later on you know Roy Palmer played baritone, cornet, trombone, a lot of instruments. He was a pretty good teacher. He taught a lot of people around Chicago, including myself and Lionel Hampton and Oscar Bunny Young, who I later played with at the Wisconsin Roof for about six years. And McKinley Thomas and Baritone, we had a band around there, including the singing brothers, Homer and Al Simeon. And in this band was, in time, it was Natty Dominic, you know. We played, we were close together like most of New Orleans musicians in Chicago. It was kind of cliquish, you know. Just like Joe and Manuel and Freddie. Every time Joe Oliver wanted Trump to play, I called him to play, he sent him to New Orleans and that one, you know. And so that's what they would do. And they stuck together for quite a while. And until they began to have internal strife, I say, you know. They began to disagree with one another. That was the beginning of Joe Oliver's great band. Some kind of disagreement concerning recordings. Joe used to record under assumed names sometimes, you know. And so I heard that Joe, he changed. He used Eddie Atkinson in the place of Dufres, and he used Jimmy Noon in the place of Jam, Johnny Dodge.
